Looking for a Used Scooter Exporter in Taiwan?

Taiwan is one of the largest sources of well-maintained used scooters in the world — but not every exporter can back that up with a real yard, real inspection, and a real export track record. Here's what a legitimate wholesale supplier looks like, and how the process actually works.
Why Taiwan for used scooters

Taiwan has one of the highest scooter-ownership rates on earth, and every registered vehicle is subject to mandatory periodic inspection. That combination — a huge fleet, disciplined maintenance culture, and government-enforced upkeep — produces a steady supply of used scooters with detailed service history and comparatively low mileage per year of registration.
For wholesale buyers in Africa, the Middle East, and other emerging markets, that translates into lower breakdown rates after import and stronger resale value for your customers.
What a legitimate exporter actually does
Sourcing. Units are bought from Taiwan's domestic used-vehicle market, not assembled on demand from unrelated sellers.
Inspection & grading. Every scooter is checked and assigned a condition grade (A/B/C) before it's offered for export — engine condition, body wear, and cosmetic damage are all documented.

Model selection. Buyers choose brands, models, and quantities. Mixing several models in one container is standard practice — it lets you test demand across different customer segments instead of betting the whole order on one model.
Container loading. Units are loaded into a 40HQ container, often using SKD (Semi Knocked Down) packing — handlebars and front wheels removed — to fit more units per container without damage.
Documentation & shipping. A full document set — commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading — ships with the container so customs clearance at destination goes smoothly.

A container-load supplier is different from a used-parts reseller or a single-unit dealer. If an exporter can't show you a real inventory yard or pre-shipment inspection photos, that's a red flag — not a shortcut.

Taiwan Motorcycle Wholesale MOQ: What Buyers Need to Know

Almost every wholesale motorcycle inquiry starts with the same question: what's the minimum, and can it be lower? Here's what MOQ actually means for a container-load export order, and how to plan around it.
What "MOQ" means in this context

MOQ — minimum order quantity — is the smallest quantity a supplier will process as one order. For Taiwan used motorcycle export, buyers can choose between 50 units per 20FT container or 125 units per 40HQ container. Neither number is a sales tactic to push bigger orders; both are set by how many motorcycles physically fit in that container size once they're packed and secured for ocean freight. See the Container Loading Guide for how to choose between the two.
Why not a smaller order?

Ocean freight is priced by the container, not by the unit. Shipping fewer than a full container load means paying full-container freight for partial-container cargo — the per-unit cost goes up sharply, and for a low-margin, high-volume product like a used scooter, that math rarely works for either side. Full-container orders are also what makes pre-shipment inspection, SKD (Semi Knocked Down) packing, and consolidated documentation efficient to run.

Used motorcycles and scooters are quoted FOB Kaohsiung at roughly US$185–900 per unit, depending on model, year and condition grade. Used cars are quoted at roughly US$1,880–4,680 per unit. These are indicative ranges, not fixed prices: the final quotation is sent together with the current stock list for the exact units you choose.
How to reach the MOQ without over-committing to one model
The MOQ applies to the container, not to any single model. Buyers routinely mix models to hit either the 50-unit or 125-unit threshold:
Pick 3–5+ models across brands (KYMCO, Yamaha, SYM, AEON, PGO) to spread risk and match different price points in your market — fewer models for a 20FT order, more for a 40HQ.

Allocate quantities per model based on what sells fastest in your territory — on a 40HQ order, a typical spread might be 25–40 units of a few proven sellers and smaller batches of 10–20 to test new models.
Leave room for spare parts if useful — fast-moving items like tires, brake pads, spark plugs, and filters can often be consolidated into the same container.
Confirm the final mix with your supplier before deposit, so grading and photos are prepared for the exact units you're ordering. See the Grading Standard Guide for how condition grades work.

Mixing models isn't just a way to hit the MOQ — most experienced buyers prefer it. A container with 3+ models lets you test demand across your customer base instead of betting the full order on one bike.
Cars run on a different MOQ

If you're sourcing both motorcycles and cars, note that used cars are a separate order with a separate MOQ: 5 units per 40HQ container, since a standard 40HQ holds roughly 5 passenger cars. The two categories are quoted and loaded independently. See the full model list for both on the catalog page.

How Many Motorcycles Fit in a Container?

Before committing to an order, most buyers want the same answer: exactly how many units they're getting for their money. Here's how motorcycle and car loading actually works across the two container sizes Luckwell ships.
Two container options for motorcycles
Luckwell ships used motorcycles in two container sizes, and the unit count scales with the container's volume:
20FT container
~50 units — lower upfront commitment, better for testing a new market
40HQ container
~125 units — better per-unit freight cost, standard for repeat buyers
Used cars are only shipped by 40HQ, holding approximately 5 units — there's no 20FT option for cars, since a 20FT container can't hold enough passenger vehicles to justify the freight cost.
Why a 40-foot high-cube, not a standard 40-foot?

The extra ceiling height of a 40HQ over a standard 40FT container matters once motorcycles are stacked — it allows an additional tier to be packed safely without exceeding weight distribution limits, which is where most of the jump from 50 to 125 units comes from rather than length alone.
How motorcycles are packed: SKD
Motorcycles aren't loaded fully assembled and upright the way they'd sit in a showroom. Luckwell uses SKD (Semi Knocked Down) packing to fit the stated unit count per container:
Handlebars folded or turned parallel to the frame to reduce width.
Front wheel detached on most models and secured alongside the unit.
Units stacked in rows, front-to-back and interlocked where the model allows, using the full container height.
Straps and dunnage secure each row so units don't shift during ocean transit.

SKD is not the same as a full CKD (Completely Knocked Down) kit — motorcycles arrive substantially assembled. Reattaching the handlebar and front wheel on arrival typically takes a few minutes per unit with basic tools.
Choosing between 20FT and 40HQ
The right container size depends on how you plan to sell, not just budget:
Choose 20FT (50 units) if you're entering a new territory, testing which models sell before scaling up, or your capital is better spent ordering more frequently in smaller batches.

Choose 40HQ (125 units) if you have proven, repeat demand — the per-unit freight cost drops meaningfully at this volume, and it supports mixing 5+ models in one shipment. See the Wholesale MOQ Guide for how buyers typically split a 125-unit order across models.
How many motorcycles fit in a 40HQ container?

A 40HQ (40-foot high-cube) container holds approximately 125 used motorcycles when packed using SKD (Semi Knocked Down) methods — handlebars turned or removed and front wheels detached to reduce width, then stacked in rows.
How many motorcycles fit in a 20FT container?
A standard 20FT container holds approximately 50 used motorcycles, packed the same SKD way as a 40HQ but at roughly 40% of the volume.
Should I order a 20FT or a 40HQ container?

A 20FT/50-unit order suits buyers testing a new market or ordering less frequently, since it lowers the upfront commitment. A 40HQ/125-unit order has a better per-unit freight cost and is the standard choice for buyers with steady, repeat demand.
Can used cars be loaded into a 20FT container?
No. Used cars are only ordered by 40HQ container, holding approximately 5 units. Cars do not have a 20FT option because the per-unit freight cost would be too high at that volume.

Grading Standard
Taiwan Used Motorcycle Grading Standard: A/B/C Explained
You can't inspect a container in person before it ships. Here's the grading system Luckwell uses so you know exactly what condition you're buying, before you commit.
Why grading matters for wholesale buyers

When you're ordering 50+ units sight-unseen from another country, "used" isn't specific enough to price or resell against. Every motorcycle and car Luckwell exports is assigned a condition grade — A, B, or C — based on a pre-shipment inspection, so you know what you're paying for before the container leaves Kaohsiung.
Who inspects, and when

Grading is done by Luckwell's own team in Kaohsiung, not self-reported by the previous owner. Inspection happens before a unit is confirmed for your order — so the grade you're quoted is the grade you're shipped, not an estimate made at the point of original purchase years earlier.
Engine check — starts, idles, and runs without abnormal noise or excessive smoke.
Body and cosmetic review — paint condition, rust, dents, and how much of the original bodywork remains.
Functional parts — lights, brakes, and controls are tested for basic function.
Grade assigned — the unit is logged as A, B, or C and photographed for the buyer's record.
How grading affects pricing and your order mix

Grade is priced into every unit — Grade A costs more per unit than Grade C, reflecting the cosmetic condition and resale value it supports in your market. Most wholesale buyers don't order a single grade across the whole container; instead they mix grades to match different price points among their own customers, the same way they mix models to reach the container MOQ (see the Wholesale MOQ Guide).
The same A/B/C standard applies to both motorcycles and cars, so if you're ordering a mixed shipment, you're comparing condition on one consistent scale across categories — not two different systems.

What does Grade A, B, and C mean for a used motorcycle?

Grade A means excellent engine condition with minor cosmetic wear and 90%+ original body condition. Grade B means good running condition with moderate cosmetic wear like scratches or faded paint. Grade C means functional condition with visible cosmetic wear or minor body damage, priced accordingly.
Who grades the vehicles, and when?
Every unit is pre-shipment inspected by Luckwell's own team in Kaohsiung before it's confirmed for a container, not self-reported by the original owner or a third party the buyer can't verify.
Does grading apply to both motorcycles and cars?
Yes. The same A/B/C grading system is used for both used motorcycles and used cars, so buyers ordering a mixed container can compare condition across categories using one consistent standard.
Can I see photos or an inspection report before ordering?

Yes. Photos and grade notes are provided for the units allocated to an order before the balance payment is due, so buyers can confirm condition matches the agreed grade before the container is loaded.

Inspection Checklist
How to Inspect Used Scooters Before Export
You can't test-ride a container. Here's the checklist that determines whether a unit ships at all, and what grade it's assigned — so you know what to ask for from any exporter, not just Luckwell.
The five checkpoints
Engine
Starts cold, idles steady, no abnormal knocking or excessive smoke on startup
Frame & VIN
VIN matches documentation, no frame cracks, rust limited to surface level
Electrical
Headlight, taillight, indicators, horn, and ignition all function
Tires & brakes
Tread depth and brake response checked; noted if replacement is needed on arrival
Cosmetic condition
Paint, plastics, and seat condition assessed — this is what separates Grade A from B/C
These same checks feed directly into the condition grade assigned to each unit — see the Grading Standard Guide for how A/B/C is defined.
Who does the inspection, and when
Sourcing — units are pulled from inventory to match the buyer's confirmed model and quantity list.
Inspection — each unit goes through the five checkpoints above, done by the exporter's own team, not the previous owner's word.
Grading & photos — a grade (A/B/C) is assigned and photos are taken per unit.
Buyer review — photos and grade notes are sent to the buyer before the balance payment, as a checkpoint before the container is loaded.
Loading — once confirmed, units are SKD-packed and loaded.

Ask any exporter directly: who performs the inspection, and do you receive photos before the balance is due? If the answer is vague, that's the real risk in a sight-unseen wholesale order — not the vehicles themselves.
Third-party inspection option

Buyers who want an additional layer of verification can arrange their own third-party inspection (for example, through SGS or a local agent in Taiwan) at their own cost, run alongside the exporter's own report. This is optional and most repeat buyers don't use it once they've verified a supplier's inspection reports match what arrives — but it's a reasonable step for a first order at a larger volume.
What does a pre-shipment inspection check on a used scooter?

A full inspection covers the engine (starting, idle, smoke, noise), frame and VIN, electrical system (lights, horn, ignition), tires and brakes, and cosmetic condition — the same checks that determine the unit's A/B/C grade.
Can I request my own third-party inspection before shipping?

Yes. Buyers are welcome to arrange a third-party inspection (such as SGS or a local agent) at their own cost before the balance payment, in addition to the exporter's own pre-shipment inspection report.
What documentation should I receive after inspection?

Photos of each unit, a condition grade (A/B/C), and notes on any mechanical or cosmetic issues found. This is provided before the balance payment is due, so it can be checked against the agreed order.
Does inspection happen before or after the deposit is paid?

Units are sourced and inspected after the deposit confirms the order, then photos and grade notes are sent before the balance payment and container loading — giving buyers a checkpoint before committing the full amount.

Why buyers choose Taiwan

Taiwan requires mandatory annual vehicle inspection and has one of the highest scooter-ownership rates in the world, producing a large fleet of small-displacement scooters with traceable service history. For markets where the demand is everyday commuter transport rather than larger-displacement bikes, Taiwan's fleet composition and lower average price point are usually the better fit — see the Used Motorcycle Supplier for Africa guide for how this plays out in Luckwell's current markets.
Where Japan tends to fit better

Japan's export trade covers a broader range of displacements and model types, sourced largely through established auction systems with their own standardized grading. Buyers building out a product line that includes larger-displacement or more specialized models often look to Japan for that segment, sometimes alongside a Taiwan supplier covering the small-displacement, higher-volume end of the same market.

Many established wholesale buyers don't pick one country exclusively — they source everyday commuter scooters from Taiwan and larger or specialty models from Japan, matching each source to the segment it's strongest in.

What's the main difference between Taiwan and Japan as used motorcycle export sources?

Taiwan's fleet is dominated by small-displacement scooters (50cc–180cc) sold directly by exporters at a fixed wholesale MOQ. Japan's export fleet includes a wider mix of displacements and is typically sourced through auction houses using Japan's own condition-grading system, often at higher average price points.
Which source is better for African and Middle Eastern buyers?

It depends on the target vehicle type. Buyers looking for everyday small-displacement scooters at a lower price point per unit typically favor Taiwan; buyers looking for larger-displacement or specialty models often look to Japan, sometimes sourcing from both to cover different segments of their local market.
Is Taiwan's grading system the same as Japan's?

No. Taiwan exporters like Luckwell use an A/B/C grading standard set by the individual exporter's own pre-shipment inspection. Japan's export trade commonly references auction-house or inspection-body grading scales, which are standardized across many Japanese exporters rather than set by one company.
Does Taiwan or Japan have a lower MOQ for a first order?
Taiwan wholesale exporters like Luckwell offer a 50-unit 20FT container option specifically to lower the entry point for first-time or smaller buyers, alongside the standard 125-unit 40HQ order.
